pages.text: The Cloud That Wouldn't Rain: A science mystery about condensation, clouds, and rain

Lila loved the school garden, but this week the bean plants were drooping and the soil felt dry. Above the garden hung one giant gray cloud that looked full of rain, yet not a single drop fell. Lila stared up in her yellow raincoat while her friend Arun crossed his arms and studied the sky beside her. “How can a cloud look that full and still not rain?” he asked. The question followed them all day. After science club, they decided to solve the mystery instead of just waiting for the weather to explain itself.

In science club, Lila and Arun filled a bowl with warm water and held a tray of ice above it. Tiny droplets quickly formed underneath the cold tray and began to drip back down. “That looks like rain!” Lila said. Their teacher explained that warm water turns into water vapor, and when that vapor cools, it condenses into tiny drops—just like inside a cloud. A cloud rains only when enough droplets join together and grow heavy. Later that evening, cooler air finally moved in, and the cloud over the garden let go of a soft, steady rain. Arun smiled through the window. “So the cloud wasn’t empty,” he said. “It just wasn’t ready yet.”

Water vapor Warm water can change into an invisible gas called water vapor. Condensation When water vapor cools, it turns back into tiny liquid drops. Rain Drops fall when they grow too heavy to stay in the cloud. What the Story Teaches Clouds are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals. Water from lakes, soil, and plants can turn into water vapor and rise into the air. When that vapor cools, it condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. Rain begins when many small droplets join together and become heavy enough to fall to the ground.

THE END Sometimes the sky keeps its secrets—until science helps you see them. Science mysteries begin when someone notices something surprising and asks why. Looking closely, testing ideas, and learning from the results can turn a puzzle into understanding.
